passage: In the village school near Mangaluru, Francis waited for his turn to recite the poem. His breath was coming fast and high, little sips of air, and his hands were cold. He remembered what his grandmother said when the cows got restless: slow and low. So he put a hand on his belly, breathed in, then out, longer. Once. Twice. His chest stopped fluttering. That afternoon, when Jatin snatched his cricket bat, the fast breathing came back, hot this time. Francis noticed it. He breathed out slowly before speaking. "Give it back, it's my turn." His voice came out steady. Walking home past the paddy fields, he thought, I can change my breathing. I can change how I feel.

qa.q: Where did Francis put his hand?
qa.a: Francis put a hand on his belly.

qa.q: How did Francis feel walking home past the paddy fields?
qa.a: Francis felt hopeful and more confident, realising he could change his breathing and so change how he felt.

qa.q: How did slowing his breath help with Jatin?
qa.a: It let Francis speak steadily and ask for the bat back instead of snapping in anger.

qa.q: How might Jatin see Francis's steady voice?
qa.a: Jatin might be surprised that Francis stayed calm, which makes a fight less likely.

grounding: A schoolchild notices fast, shallow breath when nervous and when angry, and gains a sense of control by slowing it.

passage:
Backstage at the school music night in Bergen, Ingrid's breath was racing. She could feel it high in her chest, quick and shallow, as if she'd been running, though she'd only been standing. Her little brother Paulo poked his head round the curtain. "You look weird."
"I'm breathing too fast," Ingrid said, surprised she knew. In class, Mr Dahl had shown them how to breathe out for longer than in, like cooling hot chocolate. She tried it. Out, slowly. Again. Her shoulders dropped, and her fingers stopped trembling on the sheet music.
She played her piece with only one wrong note. Afterwards, eating waffles, she told Paulo, "I can turn my breathing down, like a volume knob."
"Show me," he said.

qa.q: Where was Ingrid when her breath was racing?
qa.a: Backstage at the school music night in Bergen.

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel after the performance?
qa.a: Ingrid felt pleased and in control, comparing her breathing to a volume knob she could turn down.

qa.q: What could Ingrid try the next time she feels nervous?
qa.a: Ingrid could notice the quick, shallow breathing early and breathe out longer than in, as she did backstage.

qa.q: Why might Paulo want Ingrid to show him?
qa.a: Paulo saw Ingrid go from looking weird to playing well, so he may want the same trick for his own nerves.

grounding: A child notices fast, shallow breath when nervous and learns that slowing it quiets the body and brings a sense of control.

passage: Thabo came into the Johannesburg kitchen to find his sister Vera riding his new bike round the yard. 'That's MINE!' His chest was heaving. His breath came fast and short, like he'd been running, though he hadn't. He was about to yank her off. Then he remembered what the swimming coach said about breath and nerves. He noticed it: fast, high, tight. He stopped at the door and breathed out long, like blowing a candle out slowly. Once. Twice. Five times. His chest softened. His fists opened. 'Vera. Can you give it back, please? I haven't even ridden it yet.' She rolled her eyes but got off. Thabo felt oddly proud. He had steered his own body, like steering a bike.

qa.q: Who was riding Thabo's new bike?
qa.a: His sister Vera.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he saw Vera on his bike?
qa.a: He was angry, with his breath coming fast and short and his chest heaving.

qa.q: What did Thabo try, and why did it help?
qa.a: He noticed his fast breath and breathed out long five times, which calmed his body so he could ask Vera calmly.

qa.q: How might Vera have reacted if Thabo had yanked her off?
qa.a: She might have been hurt or shouted back, and the fight would have got bigger.

grounding: Shows a child noticing fast, shallow breath when angry and slowing it, gaining a sense of control over his body.

passage: At the inter-school spelling bee in the auditorium, Minakshi waited in the row of chairs on stage. Her breath was coming in quick little gasps high in her chest. Her hands were cold. Hrithik Sir, the teacher in charge, bent down beside her chair. 'Notice your breathing?' Minakshi nodded. 'Quick.' 'Try this. Breathe in through your nose for three, out through your mouth for five.' She did it three times. Her shoulders dropped. The quick gasps slowed into longer breaths. When her name was called, she walked to the mic. Her voice wobbled on the first word, then steadied. 'Rhythm. R-H-Y-T-H-M.' Back in her chair, she thought, I did that. I made my body calm down.

qa.q: What word did Minakshi spell?
qa.a: Rhythm.

qa.q: How was Minakshi feeling while waiting on stage?
qa.a: She was nervous, with quick gasps high in her chest and cold hands.

qa.q: What small step did Hrithik Sir suggest?
qa.a: Breathing in through the nose for three and out through the mouth for five.

qa.q: How might Hrithik Sir feel seeing Minakshi calm herself?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased that his small tip helped her take control.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild noticing fast, shallow breathing when nervous and learning slow breathing to quiet the body and feel in control.

passage:
Monday: Avni, nine, stormed in from the colony park after a fight over the swing. Nirmala Dadi saw her chest going up and down fast. 'Put your hand on your chest, Avni. What's your breath doing?' 'Running,' Avni muttered.
Wednesday: Before her dance recital, Avni noticed it herself. Quick, shallow breaths. She remembered Dadi's words, 'long out-breath, like cooling tea,' and tried it in the wings. The flutter settled a little.
Saturday: Her cousin broke her crayons. Avni's breath started racing. This time she stopped, blew out slowly three times and only then said, 'That makes me cross.' Later she told Dadi, 'I can make my breath slow down myself.'

qa.q: What did Avni say her breath was doing on Monday?
qa.a: Running.

qa.q: How did Avni feel on Saturday when she said she could slow her breath herself?
qa.a: She felt proud and in control, pleased that she could calm her own body.

qa.q: What did Nirmala Dadi do that started the change?
qa.a: She asked Avni to notice her breath with a hand on her chest and taught her a long out-breath.

qa.q: How might Avni's cousin have been affected by her calm words?
qa.a: The cousin probably felt less scared than if Avni had shouted, and could hear that she was cross.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild learning over several days to notice fast breathing when angry or nervous and slow it, gaining a sense of control.

passage: Irawati, you say your breath goes fast when you're cross with your brother? Let your Vinita Aaji tell you something. When I was in Class 4, at our school in Nagpur, I had to recite a poem at assembly. My breath went quick and shallow, like a sparrow's, and my hands shook. When I was angry with my sister, the same thing: fast, fast, fast. My teacher, Kulkarni Bai, noticed. She put my hand on my belly and said, 'Make this rise slowly, and let the air out even slower, like cooling tea.' I tried it behind the curtain. My breath slowed, and so did my heart. I recited the whole poem. After that I knew my body would listen to me if I asked it gently.

qa.q: What did Kulkarni Bai tell young Vinita to do?
qa.a: Make the belly rise slowly and let the air out even slower, like cooling tea.

qa.q: How did young Vinita feel before reciting?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with quick, shallow breath and shaking hands.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
qa.a: The teacher noticing and teaching slow belly breathing, which calmed her body so she could recite the whole poem.

qa.q: How might Kulkarni Bai have felt watching Vinita recite?
qa.a: Kulkarni Bai was probably proud and pleased that the simple breathing had helped.

grounding: A grandmother recalls noticing her fast breath as a nervous schoolchild and learning that slow breathing quiets the body.
